qt: to the Commission Thomas Pellerin-Carlin (S&D), Nora Mebarek (S&D), Aurore Lalucq (S&D), Raphaël Glucksmann (S&D), Pierre Jouvet (S&D), Jean-Marc Germain (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Emma Rafowicz (S&D), Murielle Laurent (S&D) Subject:

Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heatwaves in the EU. This resulted in May 2026 becoming the hottest May on record in France. Workers in environments that are highly exposed to heat, such as agriculture, construction, industry, logistics and the maintenance of public spaces, face growing health and safety risks. According to the International Labour Organization, heat-related deaths in the workplace have increased by 42 % since 2000. While Directive 89/391/EEC imposes a general obligation on employers to protect the health and safety of their workers, it does not establish specific provisions with regard to the risks from extreme heatwaves. In light of the above: 1.
In the short term, what steps does the Commission intend to take?
Will the European framework law on adaptation to climate change require plans for the adaptation of working conditions to be established at sector and company level?
Will the Quality Jobs Act impose binding measures concerning the adaptation of working conditions in the event of extreme heatwaves?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.10.2026) The EU has strong rules addressing occupational safety and health (OSH) risks, including heat-related risks. Directive 89/391/EEC includes a general obligation for employers to assess and address all OSH risks in light of the specific circumstances of each workplace. Other directives1 contain detailed provisions on indoor temperatures and inclement weather. The Commission and the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) provide guidance and practical tools2. The Commission expects to adopt in October 2026, as part of its new framework for climate resilience, a proposal for a new European Climate Resilience Law. It will establish new obligations on public authorities, but not on companies, and it will be up to the Member States to determine their climate resilience objectives and the measures needed to achieve them. As regards the Quality Jobs Act, the second-stage consultation of the social partners ran until 28 September 20263. In parallel, the Commission is gathering additional evidence, including from other stakeholders and the wider public4. One of the topics put to consultation is risks related to inclement weather conditions and high temperatures. Policy measures could address them as part of an existing obligation to conduct a risk assessment as set in Directive 89/391/EEC, or by exploring how to better address heat- and weather-related OSH risks in ways that are also proportionate to the means of influence of the employer.
